section.title: The High Priestly Prayer
section.sectionRationale: The Upper Room Discourse closes as Jesus turns from His disciples to His Father in the longest recorded prayer of His life. On the threshold of the cross He prays for His own glorification, for the protection, joy, and sanctification of His disciples, and for the unity and final glory of all who will believe through their message. It is a window into the heart of the Son and His mediating love for His people.
section.thesis: On the eve of the cross Jesus prays that the Father would glorify the Son so the Son may glorify the Father and give eternal life to His own, and He intercedes for His disciples and for all who will believe, that they may be kept, sanctified in the truth, made one as the Father and Son are one, and finally be with Him to see His glory.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Jesus prays for His own glorification and the giving of eternal life; He prays for His disciples, that they be protected, filled with joy, and sanctified in the truth and sent into the world; and He prays for all future believers, that they may be one and at last be with Him to behold His glory.

units.label: Prayer for the Son
units.note: glorify Your Son that He may glorify You

verses.text: When Jesus had spoken these things, He lifted up His eyes to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come. {{doxazo|Glorify}} Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You.
For You granted Him authority over all people, so that He may give eternal life to all those You have given Him.
Now this is {{zoe|eternal life}}, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent.
I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do.
And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed.

units.label: Prayer for the disciples
units.note: keep them, sanctify them, send them

verses.text: I have revealed Your name to those You have given Me out of the world. They were Yours; You gave them to Me, and they have kept Your word.
Now they know that everything You have given Me comes from You.
For I have given them the words You gave Me, and they have received them. They knew with certainty that I came from You, and they believed that You sent Me.
I ask on their behalf. I do not ask on behalf of the world, but on behalf of those You have given Me; for they are Yours.
All I have is Yours, and all You have is Mine; and in them I have been glorified.
I will no longer be in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to You. Holy Father, protect them by Your name, the name You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one.
While I was with them, I protected and preserved them by Your name, the name You gave Me. Not one of them has been lost, except the son of destruction, so that the Scripture would be fulfilled.
But now I am coming to You; and I am saying these things while I am in the world, so that they may have My joy fulfilled within them.
I have given them Your word and the world has hated them. For they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.
I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one.
They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.
{{hagiazo|Sanctify}} them by the {{aletheia|truth}}; Your word is truth.
As You sent Me into the world, I have also sent them into the world.
For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified by the truth.

units.label: Prayer for all believers
units.note: that they may all be one

verses.text: I am not asking on behalf of them alone, but also on behalf of those who will believe in Me through their message,
that all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You. May they also be in Us, so that the world may believe that You sent Me.
I have given them the glory You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one,
I in them and You in Me, that they may be perfectly united, so that the world may know that You sent Me and have loved them just as You have loved Me.
Father, I want those You have given Me to be with Me where I am, that they may see the glory You gave Me because You loved Me before the foundation of the world.
Righteous Father, although the world has not known You, I know You, and they know that You sent Me.
And I have made Your name known to them and will continue to make it known, so that the love You have for Me may be in them, and I in them.”

doxazo.gloss: To glorify. The prayer opens and returns to glory: the Father glorify the Son so the Son may glorify the Father, and restore to the Son the glory He had before the world existed. The hour of the cross is the hour of mutual glorification, where the Father's love and the Son's obedience shine, and through which the Son gives eternal life.

zoe.gloss: Life, eternal life. Jesus defines it not as mere endless existence but as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent. Eternal life is relational and present, a knowing of God in Christ that begins now and lasts forever, the very gift the Son was given authority to grant to all the Father gave Him.

hagiazo.gloss: To sanctify, set apart as holy, consecrate. Jesus prays that the Father sanctify the disciples by the truth, and He sanctifies Himself, sets Himself apart to the cross, for their sake. Sanctification here is both being set apart for God's service in the world and being made holy through the truth of God's word.

aletheia.gloss: Truth. Jesus prays, sanctify them by the truth, and adds, Your word is truth. God's word is the means by which His people are set apart and made holy, the reliable revelation that shapes them for God. The same truth is embodied in Christ, so that to be sanctified in the truth is to be conformed to Him.

basic.context: Having finished teaching His disciples, Jesus prays aloud to His Father, and John lets us listen in. First He prays for Himself: the hour has come, so let the Father glorify the Son and the Son glorify the Father, and let the Son give eternal life, which is knowing God. Then He prays for His disciples: that the Father would protect them in a hostile world, fill them with His joy, sanctify them by the truth, and send them out as He was sent. Finally He prays for all who will ever believe through the apostles' message, that they may be one as the Father and Son are one, and that they may be with Him to see His glory.
basic.hermeneutics: This is Jesus interceding, a glimpse into His high priestly heart. The key questions are, what does Jesus most want for His people, and what is eternal life. He wants them kept, made holy, made one, and finally brought to be with Him. Eternal life is defined relationally: knowing the true God and Jesus Christ. Note that Jesus does not ask that His people be removed from the world but kept in it and sent into it, sanctified for mission.
basic.originalLanguages: The prayer circles around key words. Jesus asks the Father to doxazo, glorify, the Son so the Son may glorify the Father. He defines zoe, eternal life, as knowing God and the one He sent. He prays hagiazo, sanctify them, by the aletheia, the truth, which is God's word.
basic.typology: Jesus here fulfills the role of the high priest who intercedes for the people, bearing them on His heart before God, a role the temple priests only foreshadowed. His prayer for unity fulfills the hope of one people of God gathered under one head.
basic.christ: Christ is the eternal Son who shared the Father's glory before the world existed, the one given authority to grant eternal life, and the great High Priest who prays for His people and sanctifies Himself for them. He longs for them to be with Him and to see His glory.
basic.god: God the Father is holy and righteous, the only true God, who loves the Son, gave a people to Him, and loves those people as He loves the Son. The prayer reveals the intimate life of Father and Son into which believers are drawn.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 7 presents Christ interceding as High Priest. John 1 spoke of the Word's glory before creation. Ephesians 4 urges the unity Jesus prays for. 1 John 3 speaks of seeing Him and being like Him.
basic.oneStory: On the edge of the cross, the Son prays as our great High Priest, asking that His people be kept, made holy, made one, and finally brought to be with Him in glory. The prayer gathers the whole purpose of redemption: to draw a people into the love and glory the Father and Son have shared from before the world began.

context.literary:
The prayer is the only place in the Gospel where a whole chapter is spoken to the Father, and its design repays slow reading. It moves in widening circles: Jesus prays for Himself, verses 1 to 5, for the eleven, verses 6 to 19, and for all who will believe through their word, verses 20 to 26. The centre of gravity is the middle section, but the outer circles keep returning to it. The Son's glory frames the prayer, since it opens with 'glorify Your Son' and closes with the wish that they 'see the glory You gave Me,' verse 24. Love frames it as well: the last verse speaks of the love the Father has for the Son being in the disciples, and the first movement of the Gospel's argument, 1:18, had already placed the Son in the Father's embrace.

The prayer is built on repeated terms. The Father 'gave' the disciples to Jesus, and the verb returns again and again. The word 'name' is revealed in verse 6, the Father's name protects in verses 11 and 12, and it is made known in verse 26. 'World' appears constantly, as the place the disciples are in but not of, verses 11 to 18. And the three addresses to the Father trace His character: simply 'Father' at the beginning, 'Holy Father' in verse 11 as Jesus asks for protection in a hostile world, and 'Righteous Father' in verse 25, as He sums up the contrast between the world that does not know God and the Son who does.

The prayer also echoes the language of the whole Gospel. Verse 1 picks up the 'hour' that the Gospel has been waiting for since 2:4 and which was announced in 12:23 and 13:1. Verse 4 states the work is done, while the cross is still ahead, using a verb that comes back at 19:28 and 19:30. And the prayer is placed between the last words in the upper room and the crossing of the Kidron in 18:1, so it functions as a threshold. The 'high priestly' title is a later one, not John's, but it fits the way the chapter intercedes, consecrates and offers.
context.historical:
The setting is the night of Passover, probably in or near the upper room, with the arrest in a garden across the Kidron only moments away, 18:1. Jesus lifts His eyes to heaven, which was a Jewish posture of prayer, though the text says He prays aloud, so that the disciples hear what He asks, verse 13. They are given the words to hold onto when they are scattered.

The imagery draws on the practice of Israel's high priest. Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, he entered the Most Holy Place and made atonement for himself, his household and the whole assembly, Leviticus 16:17. On his breastpiece he carried the names of the sons of Israel over his heart 'as a continual reminder before the LORD,' Exodus 28:29, and on his forehead a plate engraved 'HOLY TO THE LORD,' Exodus 28:36. Before he served, he was consecrated by a ritual of washing, clothing and sacrifice, Exodus 29:1. John never calls Jesus a priest in this chapter, but the elements are all present: He bears His people before the Father, He consecrates Himself for them, verse 19, and He prays that they will be kept by the Father's name. That last phrase recalls the priestly blessing in which Aaron's sons were to 'put My name' on the people of Israel, Numbers 6:24 to 27, a blessing that begins 'the LORD bless you and keep you.'

The disciples' situation matches the prayer. The synagogue ban has been mentioned in 16:2, and the world's hatred, which Jesus names in verse 14, was real in the first century. Jesus' request that they be kept 'from the evil one,' verse 15, reflects a world in which opposition, whether from authorities or from the powers behind them, was a daily possibility. The mention of Judas as 'the son of destruction,' verse 12, shows that Jesus is thinking of a specific loss that has already happened in the plan. He does not pray over the failure as an accident, but as something the Scripture anticipated, and he sets it beside the faithful eleven.
context.canonical:
The prayer gathers up every major strand of Israel's hope and gives each a new centre. The name of God, which Moses asked to know and which God proclaimed in Exodus 34:5 to 7, is made known by the Son, verses 6 and 26. The glory that Moses asked to see in Exodus 33:18, and that Isaiah saw in the temple, a vision John says was of Jesus, 12:41, is the glory Jesus shared with the Father before the world existed, verse 5. The unity of God, confessed in the Shema, 'the LORD is One,' Deuteronomy 6:4, becomes the pattern for the unity of His people, verses 11, 21 and 22.

The New Testament picks up the prayer in several directions. Hebrews says Jesus is a priest who 'always lives to intercede for' those who draw near to God, Hebrews 7:25, and that He appears 'on our behalf in the presence of God,' Hebrews 9:24. Paul says the risen Christ 'is interceding for us,' Romans 8:34, and 1 John 2:1 names Him an advocate with the Father. All of these describe the continuing form of the prayer begun here. Hebrews 2:11 also uses the same verb family as verse 19 for the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified being of one family, and Hebrews 10:10 says believers 'have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.' The consecration of verse 19 is the beginning of that offering.

The prayer's unity theme runs through Ephesians 4:3 to 6, where Paul calls believers to preserve the unity of the Spirit with one Lord, one faith and one baptism, grounded in one God and Father. Its mission theme resurfaces in 20:21, where the risen Jesus says 'As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.' And its final hope, that believers will be with Him and see His glory, is fulfilled in 1 John 3:2: 'we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is,' and in the multitude before the throne and the Lamb in Revelation 7:9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John allows his readers to overhear the Son at prayer so that they will know what He wanted for them before He died. The prayer is a gift to a church that, by the time the Gospel was written, had survived the loss of the original disciples and was under pressure. John wanted them to know four things. First, that Jesus went to the cross as one who had finished a mission. He says 'I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work,' verse 4, in the past tense, before the arrest. The suffering is not a defeat that disrupts His plan. Second, that eternal life is a relationship with God and not only a duration, verse 3, and that it is already theirs. Third, that the Father keeps them. The one who prays for the disciples to be protected is the one who chose them and who 'protected and preserved' them while He was with them, verse 12. Their security does not rest on their own grip.

Fourth, and most pointedly, John wants the church to understand its calling. Jesus does not pray for escape. 'I am not asking that You take them out of the world,' verse 15. He prays that they would be sent into it as He was sent, verse 18, sanctified in the truth, verse 17, and united, verses 21 to 23, so that the world may believe and know. The unity of believers is not for its own sake. It is a public witness to the world that the Father sent the Son and loves His people. A divided or self-protective church would hide the very thing the prayer asks to reveal.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is a prayer and not a command, and it needs to be read as such. Jesus is not telling the disciples to be one, to be holy and to be sent; He is asking the Father to make them so. That should shape how the passage is applied. Unity, sanctification and mission are first received as gifts. Believers are not issued a set of tasks to achieve unity but are invited to live out what has been prayed for and given: 'I have given them the glory You gave Me, so that they may be one,' verse 22. The ground of Christian unity is therefore something already done by Christ, which Paul echoes when he tells believers to 'preserve' the unity of the Spirit, Ephesians 4:3, rather than create it.

Some details are description of a unique moment. Jesus speaking of Himself as being about to leave the world, verse 11, and asking for the Father to glorify Him, verse 5, belong to His own situation, and believers do not pray those words for themselves. The distinction between the disciples of verses 6 to 19 and 'those who will believe through their message,' verse 20, is also one the church lives within: later believers receive the testimony of the first. What does carry over is the pattern of prayer. Believers may pray for protection from the evil one, as Jesus teaches in Matthew 6:13, for sanctification by the truth of God's word, and for the church's unity and mission, knowing that the Son prays the same for them, Hebrews 7:25.

debates.question: What kind of unity does Jesus pray for in verses 21 to 23?

views.label: Spiritual unity that already exists in Christ
views.case: The unity is the oneness of all believers in the Father and the Son, verse 21, 'May they also be in Us.' It rests on a shared life and cannot be created by human effort. The prayer is answered whenever a person is born of the Spirit and joins the one body, Ephesians 4:4. Visible division is therefore a failure to show it, not an undoing of it.

views.label: Visible, institutional unity
views.case: The prayer says the purpose is 'so that the world may believe,' verse 21, and perfect unity so that the world may know, verse 23. That means the unity must be seen. Some hold that this requires visible structures that hold the church together, because invisible unity cannot be witnessed.

views.label: Spiritual in root, visible in fruit
views.case: Most interpreters take the middle road: the unity is grounded in shared life with God, but it shows in love, shared truth and cooperation that the world can see. Jesus ties it to the way believers love each other, 13:35, and to the truth of the apostles' word, verse 20, so unity cut off from either is not what He prays for.

debates.bearing: All views agree that the unity is modeled on that of Father and Son, verses 21 and 22. The Greek uses a neuter word for one, meaning a oneness of shared life and purpose, and not a single person. A unity that ignores truth, or that has truth without love, falls short of the pattern.

debates.question: For whom does Jesus pray, and what does verse 9 mean?

views.label: Particular redemption: He prays for the elect only
views.case: Verse 9 says 'I do not ask on behalf of the world, but on behalf of those You have given Me.' Those who hold this view point to the repeated language of giving, verses 2, 6, 9 and 24, and to 6:37 and 6:39. His priestly intercession matches those for whom He dies, and the world He does not pray for in verse 9 is the world as it stays opposed to Him.

views.label: A prayer for the disciples now, with the world still in view
views.case: Verse 9 is limited to the present request for protection. The prayer later asks that 'the world may believe' and 'may know' that the Father sent Him, verses 21 and 23. Those who hold this view say Jesus does not pray for the world as a unit set against Him, but longs for people from it to come to faith, as 3:16 says God loved the world.

views.label: Two senses of 'world'
views.case: John uses 'world' for the created order loved by God, 3:16, and also for the system hostile to Him, 15:18 to 19. In verse 9 the hostile sense applies; in verses 21 and 23 the world is the field to be reached.

debates.bearing: All sides see that Jesus' intercession is real and effective and that His people are held by it. Believers can rest in being prayed for by Him, and are called to pray and witness for the world's salvation, as verses 21 and 23 set that as the goal.

debates.question: What does 'I sanctify Myself' mean in verse 19?

views.label: Consecration to sacrifice
views.case: The verb hagiazo is used for consecrating priests and offerings, as in Exodus 29. Jesus sets Himself apart for the cross, as priest and offering together. The phrase 'for them' then points to His death as a substitute, linking to Hebrews 10:10.

views.label: Consecration to His mission
views.case: Jesus says in 10:36 that the Father sanctified Him and sent Him into the world. In verse 19 He continues that setting apart, giving Himself wholly to the work, and not necessarily only in death. It parallels the disciples' sanctification and sending, verses 17 and 18.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Mission and sacrifice cannot be pulled apart. The mission is the cross, and the setting apart for it is a life of obedience to the end. Both fit the context.

debates.bearing: The verse cannot mean that Jesus needed to be made morally clean. It means His self-dedication opens the way for the disciples to be set apart in truth, as the 'so that' clause says.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word that deserves a closer look is the verb for knowing in verse 3, ginosko. Jesus defines eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ. In the Old Testament, 'to know' is regularly a word for covenant relationship and not only information. God says of Abraham that He has known him, Genesis 18:19, and Hosea laments that Israel has no knowledge of God while keeping religious practices. In the Gospel the same verb marks the shared life between Father and Son in 10:14 and 15: 'I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father.' To say eternal life is to know God is to say it is a participation in that relationship. The phrase 'only true God' also echoes the confession of the Shema and sets the Father against every false god, while the phrase 'Jesus Christ, whom You have sent' places the Son inside the definition of who must be known.

The verb in verse 4, teleioo, 'accomplishing,' deserves attention. Jesus says He has completed or perfected the work the Father gave Him, in a form that stresses completion. It belongs to the family of teleo, which is the verb behind 'It is finished' in 19:30 and is used at 19:28 for everything being accomplished. The same root appears in verse 23, where the believers are 'perfectly united,' teteleiomenoi eis hen, literally perfected into one. The language connects the work of the cross, the completion of the Son's mission, with the completion of the church's unity: His work is finished so that their oneness may be brought to its goal.

The word for 'one' in verses 11, 21, 22 and 23 is the neuter hen, not the masculine heis. This is a grammatical detail with theological weight. The neuter denotes oneness of nature, purpose and life, not that the persons are the same person. John 10:30 uses the same form, 'I and the Father are one.' When Jesus prays that believers 'may be one as We are one,' He does not mean they lose individuality. He means they share a common life that is given and sustained by the Father and the Son, and that is why verse 21 says 'May they also be in Us.'

The verb tereo, 'keep' or 'protect,' in verses 11, 12 and 15 deserves notice, along with 'preserved,' phylasso, in verse 12. The Gospel uses tereo for keeping the word, verse 6, and for keeping commandments, 14:15. So the disciples keep the Father's word, verse 6, and the Father keeps them. The expression in verse 15, 'from the evil one,' ek tou ponerou, is most naturally read as personal, since the same form is used in 1 John 5:18 and 19, where 'the evil one' cannot touch the one born of God. The Lord's Prayer ends with the same expression, Matthew 6:13. In verse 12, 'the son of destruction' is huios tes apoleias, a Semitic way of describing a person by his destiny, and the same phrase is used of the man of lawlessness in 2 Thessalonians 2:3.

Finally, the pair of verbs for sending. Verse 18 uses apostello, 'As You sent Me into the world, I have also sent them,' the root of 'apostle.' The commission of 20:21 repeats the pattern, with apostello for the Father's sending of the Son and a second sending verb, pempo, for Jesus' sending of them. The disciples are therefore sent ones in the same pattern as the Son, which is why the prayer's request that they be sanctified 'in the truth' comes immediately before the commission: the one sent must be set apart by the word that sends him. The preposition en in 'sanctify them in the truth' can mean sphere or means, and both fit: the truth is the realm in which they are set apart, and also the instrument that sets them apart, since 'Your word is truth.'

typology.type: The high priest bearing the names, Exodus 28:29
typology.fulfillment: Aaron carried the names of the sons of Israel on his breastpiece over his heart whenever he entered the Holy Place. In John 17 Jesus carries the names of His own before the Father, and says 'they were Yours; You gave them to Me,' verse 6. The correspondence is that the people are brought before God by a representative who has them on his heart. The escalation is that the priest here is the Son, who has shared the Father's glory from before the world and who prays by His own right, not by borrowed office. Aaron's work had to be repeated and ended in death, Hebrews 7:23 to 25; this priest lives to intercede always. The type falls short because Aaron could carry names but not keep the people from falling.

typology.type: The Day of Atonement consecration, Leviticus 16 and Exodus 29
typology.fulfillment: On the Day of Atonement the high priest made atonement first for himself, then for the people, Leviticus 16:17, and Aaron's own consecration involved a sacrifice, Exodus 29:1. When Jesus says 'For them I sanctify Myself,' verse 19, He uses the language of consecration for the priest and the offering at once. The escalation is that He needs no atonement for Himself, Hebrews 7:26 to 27, and offers Himself, not an animal, Hebrews 9:24 to 28. The type falls short because the high priest went in once a year and then came out; Christ entered heaven itself and remains there to intercede.

typology.type: The priestly blessing and the name, Numbers 6:24 to 27
typology.fulfillment: The blessing of Numbers 6 asks that the LORD bless and keep, and puts His name on His people. Jesus' prayer that the Father would protect His own 'by Your name,' verse 11, and that He has made the name known and will keep making it known, verse 26, takes up the same language. The correspondence is of keeping under the name of God. The escalation is that the name is now disclosed fully in the Son, who says 'I have revealed Your name,' verse 6. The old blessing was spoken over Israel by priests; this one is prayed by the Son on behalf of a people drawn from every nation, Revelation 7:9. The type falls short because Israel's blessing could be forfeited by disobedience; the Son's prayer rests on His accomplished work.

typology.type: The glory before the world, Exodus 33:18 and Isaiah 6
typology.fulfillment: Moses asked to see God's glory, and Isaiah saw it in the temple. John says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory, 12:41. In this prayer, Jesus asks to return to the glory He had before the world existed, verse 5, and wants His people to see it, verse 24. The correspondence is that glory is the visible weight of God's presence. The escalation is that sight is promised to all believers, not to Moses or Isaiah alone. Moses was shown only the back of God; believers will see the Son's glory, and 1 John 3:2 adds that they will be like Him. The type falls short because the earlier visions were fleeting, and this one is final.

study.christ:
The prayer is the closest the Gospel comes to opening the inner life of the Son. Three claims about Christ in it have no parallel anywhere else in the Gospel in this concentration. The first is pre-existence. 'The glory I had with You before the world existed,' verse 5, and 'You loved Me before the foundation of the world,' verse 24. The Son is not a created being given a high office; He had glory with the Father and was loved by Him before there was a creation. This connects directly to 1:1 and 1:14, where the Word was with God in the beginning and became flesh. Philippians 2:6 to 7 says the same from the other direction, that the one who existed in the form of God emptied Himself.

The second claim is that He has authority over all people to give eternal life, verse 2. The giving is not arbitrary. It is the Father's grant of authority to the Son, and the Son's gift of life is knowing God. That is why Jesus can place Himself inside the definition of eternal life in verse 3: it is to know the Father and also Him. No prophet or priest of Israel could stand in that position. He is not only the one who shows the way to life; He is its source.

The third is His priestly work. He prays, He consecrates Himself, and He intercedes for people who are not yet born, verse 20. Hebrews tells us the prayer does not end. Jesus 'always lives to intercede,' and He appears now 'on our behalf in the presence of God,' Hebrews 9:24. Romans 8:34 draws out the comfort: the one who died and was raised is interceding, so no condemnation can stand. Believers may therefore read this chapter as a transcript of what their High Priest is still asking. What He asked then is what He asks now: that they be kept, made holy, made one, and brought home.

One caution applies. Because the priestly language is so strong, it is tempting to allegorize every detail. The text does not call Jesus a priest, and the connections with Aaron's work are drawn by Hebrews, not by John. The safest approach is to use the Aaron imagery to illuminate what the passage already says on its face: that the Son stands before the Father for His people, bearing them, consecrating Himself for them, and asking for their good. And we should notice what is distinctive. Aaron prayed in a tent made with hands; Jesus prays 'I want those You have given Me to be with Me where I am,' verse 24. This is the language of a Son's will in perfect accord with the Father's, and it answers the cry of Gethsemane. The same Jesus who will say 'not My will' in the garden here speaks with confidence because His will and the Father's are one.
study.god:
The prayer is the clearest window in the Gospel into the life of God before and beyond creation. It shows a God whose inner life is love between persons. The Father loved the Son 'before the foundation of the world,' verse 24, so God was never alone and love was never a created thing. That is why the prayer ends with the hope that the love with which the Father loved the Son 'may be in them,' verse 26. Creation and redemption flow from a love that was already complete in God, and believers are drawn into it as sharers and not merely as observers.

The prayer also shows God as holy and righteous. 'Holy Father,' verse 11, and 'Righteous Father,' verse 25, are the only places in the Gospel where Jesus addresses the Father with these adjectives, and they fit the situation. Holiness is the reason the Father is set apart from a world that does not know Him and the reason His people must be kept from it. Righteousness is the ground on which the Father judges the contrast between the world's ignorance and the Son's knowledge. In neither case does the adjective push the Father away from the Son's prayer. The holy and righteous God is the one addressed as 'Father,' and the holy name is the one by which the disciples are guarded.

God's way of keeping people is on show. The protection of verses 11 and 12 is done by the Father's name, and the Son did it while He was with them. The language of keeping is not of preventing all harm, since He asks that they be kept from the evil one, not taken from the world. The same God who allows the world to hate His people, verse 14, guards them within it. This is a sovereignty that works through the particular, with names, with a mission, and with a Son who prays for them one night before His death.

God's glory is also seen in a surprising place. The Father is glorified when the Son does the work He gave Him, verse 4, and the Son is glorified when He is lifted up. The hour of glory is the hour of the cross. This overturns the expectation that God's glory shows in power displayed above suffering, and shows that it shows in love poured out. Here the doctrine of God is bound to the doctrine of the cross, and worship is shaped by it: believers praise a God whose glory is most visible in giving Himself.

The final note is mission. The Father sends the Son, the Son sends the disciples, and the purpose is that the world may know the Father sent the Son and has loved them. God is a missionary God. His unity is displayed in His people, and His purpose is not to keep His love to Himself but to extend it. A church that has lost its outward gaze has forgotten what kind of God it worships.

crossReferences.note: The Gospel's opening for the farewell: Jesus knew His hour had come to leave this world and return to the Father, and He loved His own 'to the very end.' The prayer in chapter 17 is the speech of that love. It shows what 'to the very end' meant, intercession for them by name before the Father.

The Good Shepherd knows His sheep as the Father knows Him, and has other sheep not of this fold. The prayer for those who will believe through the apostles' message, 17:20, is the fulfillment of this promise. The one flock and one shepherd is the unity for which He now prays.

The Father gives people to the Son, and the Son loses none of them. This is the background of the language of giving in chapter 17 and the promise of keeping in verse 12. The security of the disciples rests on the will of the Father and the work of the Son together.

Aaron bore the names of Israel over his heart whenever he entered the Holy Place. The picture makes visible what Jesus does in prayer: He brings His people before the Father by name. It shows why the prayer is often called high priestly, though John does not use the title.

The priestly blessing asks that the LORD keep His people and puts His name on them. Jesus' request that the Father keep the disciples by His name picks up this vocabulary, and presents the Son as the one through whom the name is finally revealed and the blessing made secure.

Jesus 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near to God through Him. The prayer of John 17 is a sample of what this continuing intercession looks like. It assures believers that they are not prayed for once and forgotten, but are held in the Son's ongoing priestly work.

Christ Jesus, who died and was raised, is at God's right hand 'interceding for us.' Paul draws out the pastoral result: no one can condemn those for whom the risen Christ pleads. The note of confidence in John 17 becomes the argument of the end of Romans 8.

Paul tells the church to preserve the unity of the Spirit, with one body, one Spirit, one Lord and one God and Father. It reads as the working out of Jesus' prayer for unity. The oneness is already given by God, and the church's calling is to guard it in practice.

The risen Jesus says 'As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.' The commission answers the prayer of 17:18, which asks that they be sent into the world as He was. The sending in the prayer becomes the sending in the upper room after Easter.

Believers will be like Christ when they see Him as He is. This is the fulfillment of the wish in 17:24 that those given to the Son may be with Him and see His glory. John the apostle, who heard the prayer, later states the hope in his own words.

Christ existed in the form of God and emptied Himself. This passage places the same pre-existence as John 17:5 and 24, when Jesus speaks of a glory He had before the world existed. Paul shows the movement from that glory into humility, and John 17 shows it returning to glory.

A multitude too large to count, from every nation, tribe, people and tongue, stands before the throne and the Lamb. It is the picture of those 'who will believe through their message,' made visible. The prayer's final hope, that they be with Him, is the scene of the last book.

study.oneStory:
Creation began with a God who spoke and made, and who made humans in His image to know Him and to carry His rule into the world. Genesis 3 shows the breaking of that knowledge: Adam and Eve hide, and the world is filled with people who 'have not known' the Father, as Jesus says in verse 25. The rest of the Old Testament is the story of God seeking to be known again, through a name revealed to Moses, a glory over the tabernacle, a priesthood that stood between holy God and sinful people, and prophets who said that one day all would know the LORD, Jeremiah 31:34. The sacrifices and the priests carried the names of the people, but they never succeeded in making the people know God, nor in keeping them.

John 17 is where the story's turning point is stated in a prayer. The Son who had been with the Father before the world existed has come and revealed the name, verse 6. He has accomplished the work, verse 4. And the answer to the question of Genesis, how can people know God again, is given in a definition: this is eternal life, to know the only true God and the Son He sent, verse 3. Eternal life is not a prize for after death; it is the restoration of the knowledge lost in Eden, given in Christ.

The prayer also sets out what the new people will be like. They are kept by the Father's name, sanctified in His truth, united with one another as the Father and the Son are united, and sent into the world on the pattern of the Son's own sending. That is the redeemed community the whole story has been heading toward: not a nation set apart by borders, but a people drawn from every nation who share the life of God. The curse of Babel, where people scattered and could not understand one another, Genesis 11:7 to 9, is answered in the prayer for oneness, and at Pentecost the answer begins, Acts 2:5 to 11.

The prayer finally points to where the story ends. Jesus wants those given to Him to be with Him 'where I am,' to see His glory, and to share the love the Father has for the Son, verses 24 and 26. That is the new creation in the plainest terms. Revelation 21:3 says God will dwell with His people and be their God, and Revelation 22:4 says they will see His face. The glory seen only by Moses in a cleft of rock and by Isaiah in a vision becomes the ordinary sight of the redeemed. The one who prayed it the night before His death is the one who will bring it about, and so the prayer is not only a picture of what He asked but a promise of what He will bring to pass.

quiz.q: How does Jesus define eternal life in this prayer?

options.text: Knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ, whom He sent.
options.note: Verse 3 defines eternal life relationally, as knowing God in Christ.

options.text: Living forever with no more physical death.
options.note: Eternal life includes unending life, but Jesus defines it as knowing God, not merely endless duration.

options.text: Being rewarded for a good and moral life.
options.note: It is not a reward for morality but the gift of knowing God in Christ.

options.text: A restored relationship with God through Christ.
options.note: True and close, but it does not capture the precise definition, knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ.

quiz.q: What does Jesus pray for His disciples regarding the world?

options.text: Not that they be taken out of the world, but that they be kept from the evil one.
options.note: Verse 15 shows Jesus praying for protection in the world, not removal from it.

options.text: That they be removed from the world entirely.
options.note: Jesus explicitly says He is not asking that they be taken out of the world.

options.text: That they be spared all suffering in the world.
options.note: Jesus prays for their protection from the evil one, not that they be spared all hardship or removed from the world.

options.text: That they be protected as they remain in the world.
options.note: True, but it omits the specific request to be kept from the evil one.

quiz.q: How are the disciples to be sanctified, according to Jesus' prayer?

options.text: By the truth, for God's word is truth.
options.note: Verse 17 ties their sanctification to the truth of God's word.

options.text: By their own strenuous efforts to be holy.
options.note: Real holiness follows, but it is God who sanctifies them by the truth of His word, not self-effort alone.

options.text: By withdrawing from all contact with the world.
options.note: They are sanctified in the truth and sent into the world, not withdrawn from it.

options.text: By being set apart through God's word.
options.note: True, but it does not name that the word is truth, the emphasis of the verse.

quiz.q: What does Jesus pray for all who will believe through the apostles' message?

options.text: That they may be one, as the Father and Son are one, so the world may believe.
options.note: Verses 21 to 23 pray for a unity that witnesses to the world.

options.text: That they may be scattered and independent.
options.note: He prays for unity, not division.

options.text: That they may all agree on every minor detail.
options.note: The unity is a deep oneness in Christ, not mere uniformity of opinion.

options.text: That they may be united in love and truth.
options.note: True, but it omits the pattern, one as the Father and Son are one, and the aim, that the world may believe.

quiz.q: What is Jesus' final desire for those the Father has given Him?

options.text: That they be with Him where He is, to see the glory the Father gave Him.
options.note: Verse 24 expresses His longing for His people to be with Him and behold His glory.

options.text: That they be kept safe and blessed in this life.
options.note: He does pray for their keeping, but His final longing is that they be with Him to see His glory, far beyond earthly blessing.

options.text: That they achieve great success in the world.
options.note: His longing is for their presence with Him, not worldly success.

options.text: That they one day share in His presence and glory.
options.note: True, but it softens the specific longing that they be with Him where He is to see His glory.

questions: Jesus defines eternal life as knowing God. How is your relationship with God growing into a deeper knowing, not just knowing about Him?
Jesus prayed for your protection and holiness on the night before He died. How does it move you to know He was thinking of you then?
Jesus did not ask that His people be taken out of the world but kept and sent into it. How are you living as one sent into the world rather than withdrawn from it?
Jesus prayed that believers would be one so the world would believe. What is one relationship where you could pursue that unity for the sake of the gospel?
Jesus longs for you to be with Him and to see His glory. How does that final desire of His shape your hope amid present trials?

translationNotes.note: Authority over all people; the BSB footnote notes the Greek is literally all flesh. The Son is given authority over all humanity to grant eternal life to those the Father gave Him.
Protect them by Your name, the name You gave Me; the BSB footnote notes textual variation. The divine name stands for God's revealed character and covenant presence.
The son of destruction refers to Judas, whose betrayal fulfills Scripture; the phrase echoes the language later used of the man of lawlessness.
Keep them from the evil one; the BSB footnote allows or from evil. Jesus prays for protection from the devil's power rather than removal from the world.
